## Supply Chain Dynamics & Risks

- **China dominates**: ~90% of global anode production and ~98% of graphitization capacity ([Metalshub Blog](https://www.metals-hub.com/en/blog/graphite-supply-chain/)).
- **Geopolitical risks**: US anti-dumping duties (93.5% on Chinese anode graphite, July 2025), China's export permit requirements, and the EU's CBAM are reshaping sourcing strategies ([Fastmarkets Panel, June 24, 2026](https://globalevents.fastmarkets.com/lithium-battery-critical-materials-2026/panel-trade-tariffs-transformation-policy-rewriting-graphite-anode-market)).
- **Supply constraints** are emerging as the next major battery metals bottleneck, with spherical graphite prices surging over 180% since early 2024 ([Energy Metal News, May 11 & 16, 2026](https://energymetalnews.com/2026/05/11/critical-graphite-anode-supply-shortages-drive-battery-metal-prices-to-historic-peaks/)).

## Diversification & New Projects (May 2026)

- **Talga's Graphite ONE (Sweden)**: Europe's first fully integrated battery anode supply chain (mining → refining → anode production), aiming to reduce dependence on Asian processing ([Mining South East Europe, May 3, 2026](https://www.miningsee.eu/talga-graphite-one-in-sweden-europes-first-fully-integrated-battery-anode-supply-chain/)).
- **Graphite One (Ohio, US)**: A phased $435M plant targeting 10,000 mt/yr synthetic graphite processing by end of 2027, with eventual integration of Alaskan natural graphite by 2030 ([Discovery Alert](https://discoveryalert.com.au/graphite-one-ohio-anode-plant-us-graphite-supply-chain/)).
- **Africa (Mozambique, Madagascar, Tanzania)** holds ~21% of global reserves, but most material still flows to China for processing—creating a strategic gap ([Metalshub](https://www.metals-hub.com/en/blog/graphite-supply-chain/), [Mining SEE, May 16, 2026](https://www.miningsee.eu/graphite-emerges-as-europes-biggest-battery-supply-chain-weakness/)).

## Key Takeaways

- Graphite is the **most voluminous material by weight** in Li-ion battery anodes, yet has no single global price benchmark.
- The market is bifurcating between **premium synthetic graphite** (preferred by battery makers for consistency but energy-intensive) and **lower-cost natural graphite** (which requires complex purification/spheronisation).
- **Recycling** is emerging as a diversification route (EU mandates 25% recycled synthetic graphite by 2030), but currently processes <3% of demand ([Metalshub](https://www.metals-hub.com/en/blog/graphite-supply-chain/)).
- **Vertical integration** (mine-to-anode) is increasingly rewarded by investors and automakers.

---

## 📉 Supply Deficit Forecasts for 2026

All major forecasters agree on a significant deficit, though estimates vary:

| Source | Projected 2026 Deficit |
|---|---|
| **J.P. Morgan** | **330,000 tonnes** (largest gap in years) |
| **DBS Bank** | **316,000 tonnes** |
| **ICSG** | ~**150,000 tonnes** |
| **Other analysts** | Up to **>400,000 tonnes** |
| **Katusa Research / UBS** | >**400,000 tonnes** |

The deficit is structural — not cyclical — driven by a **"triple threat"** of AI data centers, electric vehicle scaling, and grid modernization colliding with a decade of mining underinvestment.

---

## 🔌 Electrification & Major Project Demand Drivers

1. **AI Data Centers** — A single large-scale AI facility requires **40,000–50,000 tonnes** of copper. AI infrastructure alone is projected to add **~110,000 tonnes** of new demand in 2026 — an **80% jump** from two years prior.

2. **Electric Vehicles** — EVs use **3–4x more copper** than conventional cars. Global EV-related copper demand is forecast to rise from ~2.6M tonnes today to **6.3M tonnes annually by 2040**.

3. **Power Grids & Renewables** — Grid and power infrastructure will account for **~60% of copper demand growth** through 2030. A 1 GW wind turbine requires ~2,866 tonnes of copper. Global demand is expected to rise from 28M to **42M tonnes by 2040** (S&P Global).

4. **Defense Spending** — NATO members have designated copper a "strategic mineral," with state-level stockpiling. Modern weapons systems, naval vessels, and drones are highly copper-intensive.

---

## ⛏️ Supply Constraints Worsening

| Issue | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Ore grades** | Below **0.6%** — half of 25 years ago |
| **Mine development timelines** | **7–17 years** from discovery to production |
| **Discovery rates** | Down **70%** since the 1990s |
| **Global inventories** | Below **3 weeks** of consumption (normal is 60–90 days) |
| **Treatment charges** | Hit **zero dollars per tonne** in 2026 — smelters paying mines for ore, unprecedented |
| **Major disruptions** | Grasberg (force majeure), Kamoa-Kakula (earthquake), El Teniente (tunnel collapse) |
| **Sulfuric acid crisis** | Strait of Hormuz tensions have choked sulfur supplies; Chile's SX-EW output hit |

---

## 💰 Price Outlook

- **2025 performance**: Copper futures gained **41%**, settling at ~$5.68/lb.
- **Early 2026**: Pushed above **$6.00/lb** in January; hit **~$12,630/tonne ($5.73/lb)** by April.
- **Goldman Sachs 2026 forecast**: ~$10,700/tonne (~$4.85/lb) — projecting a small **160,000-tonne surplus** (more bearish than consensus).
- **Consensus range**: **$5.00–$6.35/lb** (~$11,000–$14,000/tonne).
- **Long-term**: Goldman sees **$15,000/tonne by 2035**; Red Cloud sees **$6.00/lb by 2030**.

---

## ⚠️ Key Risks & Wildcards

- **US Tariffs**: A 50% tariff on semi-finished copper was implemented Aug 2025; 15% duties on all copper imports floated for 2027, potentially rising to 30% by 2028.
- **China slowdown**: China absorbs ~60% of global refined copper. Fabricator operating rates fell to ~50% (lowest since COVID).
- **Substitution risk**: High prices are incentivizing aluminum substitution where conductivity requirements allow.
- **Oil prices**: Brent above $100/barrel could reduce copper demand growth by ~1.4 percentage points (J.P. Morgan).

---

## 📊 Bottom Line

The **2026 copper market is defined by structural tension**: inelastic long-term demand from electrification, AI, and defense vs. supply constrained by depleted ore grades, underinvestment, and geopolitical disruptions. Most analysts expect the deficit to keep prices elevated, though near-term volatility from tariffs and macro headwinds is likely.

Here is a comprehensive summary of the search results covering **critical minerals recycling, substitution, exploration technology, and processing breakthroughs in 2026**:

---

## 1. Processing Breakthroughs & Recycling

### Valor – Electrochemical Liquid-Liquid Extraction (USA)
A new company launched by former Glencore executive Kunal Sinha and University of Illinois scientists Xiao Su and Johannes Elbert has commercialized a breakthrough called **electrochemical liquid-liquid extraction**. This method uses electricity-activated "molecular magnets" (ligands) to selectively bind and release target metals (gold, copper, platinum, nickel, rare earths) from ore, brine, or e-waste — without the massive energy, chemicals, or emissions of traditional smelting. Valor is building its first facility in Houston and aims to deploy modular refineries across the U.S.

### Idaho National Laboratory – Electrochemical & Bio-Based Recycling
INL researchers have advanced multiple technologies:
- **EC-Leach**: Recovers >95% of lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese from batteries using electricity instead of harsh chemicals (75% less energy, 88-90% less reagent use).
- **E-RECOV**: Room-temperature electrochemical recycling of e-waste with 75% fewer chemicals.
- **Biohydrometallurgy**: Uses microbes fed on agricultural/municipal waste to produce organic acids that break down and recover REEs, cobalt, and lithium.
- **EASE**: Ether-based aqueous separation for recovering metals from industrial wastewater and brines.

### Altilium – EcoMineral™ Process (UK)
Patented in February 2026, the **EcoMineral™ hydrometallurgical process** uses a biodegradable, near-neutral-pH lixiviant to recover copper from mine tailings. Trials at the Medet tailings site (110M tonnes) achieved up to **70% direct copper leaching efficiency**. The new spin-off ReOre Technologies will deploy this across nickel, cobalt, and manganese recovery.

### Chinese Academy of Sciences – Bio-Inspired Membrane Separation
Scientists at CAS developed a **"voltage-gated" membrane separation method** inspired by biological calcium ion channels. The 1.4-nm-wide channels force target heavy metal ions (uranium, copper, gold) into single-file, enabling selective extraction from seawater or complex mixtures. Demonstrated over 22 days of continuous operation. Potentially offers a green, chemical-free alternative for critical metal recovery.

---

## 2. Substitution

### Critical Minerals '26 Conference – Copper Substitution with Aluminium
At the **Critical Minerals '26** conference (May 2026), Martin Lynch presented evidence that approximately **70% of copper consumed globally in 2023 could have been replaced by aluminium** (wiring, cabling, tubing) without significant performance penalties. The main barrier is not technical feasibility but entrenched reputation and manufacturer reluctance.

---

## 3. Unconventional Feedstocks & Exploration

### Pacific Northwest National Laboratory – Nickel from Olivine Using Waste Acid
Published March 2026, researchers demonstrated that **waste acid** from a marine process enables more efficient extraction of nickel from olivine than commercial hydrochloric acid. The integrated process generates a nickel-iron alloy for stainless steel and produces an additional **$24 per ton of ore** — turning a previously uneconomic resource into a viable one.

### Young-Shin Jun (WashU) – Supercritical Fluid Extraction
Presented April 2026: a **supercritical CO₂-assisted extraction process** that recovers REEs from coal-based materials (unburned coals, fly ash, acid mine waste) with **nearly 100% purity** achieved by the fifth stripping stage. Also covers Ni/Co recovery from ultramafic rocks via carbonation-sulfidation.

### Granite Waste Valorisation – Magnetic Separation (Italy)
Presented at EGU 2026: researchers at Minerali Industriali srl are recovering REEs, Y, Sc, Li from **granite waste middlings** using magnetic separation. The magnetic by-product (mica-rich) hosts REE-bearing accessory phases, and process optimisation aims for near-zero-waste operations.

### Fossil Energy Waste – NETL/DOE (USA)
At the ACS Spring 2026 meeting, NETL researchers presented advanced characterization (synchrotron X-ray) of coal ash, acid mine drainage solids, and oil & gas produced waters to identify REE/Co/Ni/Sc hosting phases. A **patented step-extraction process** for REEs from coal ash has been successfully tested at pilot (barrel) scale.

---

## 4. Key Trends Across 2026

| Theme | Highlights |
|---|---|
| **Electrochemical processing** | Multiple groups (Valor, INL) using electricity instead of chemicals for high-purity separation |
| **Mine waste as feedstock** | Tailings re-processing (Altilium, granite waste, phosphate waste) becoming commercially viable |
| **Bio-inspired & bio-based** | Microbial leaching, bio-inspired membranes, biodegradable lixiviants gaining traction |
| **Substitution** | Growing recognition that aluminium can replace copper in many applications |
| **Modular/small-scale** | Shift toward smaller, simpler, field-deployable processing units vs. large smelters |

## Search Results Summary: Rare Earth Elements, China Export Controls, and Non-China Supply (May 2026)

Here is a synthesis of the most relevant findings from the search:

### 1. China's Export Control Regime (as of May 2026)

China has **significantly expanded** its rare earth export controls. Key developments:

- **May 12, 2026**: China introduced new export controls on rare earths and related technologies, barring citizens from unauthorized overseas mining. The total count of export-restricted rare earth elements reached **12** (adding holmium, erbium, thulium, europium, ytterbium to previous restrictions). ([Australian Mining Review](https://australianminingreview.com.au/news/china-tightens-rare-earth-exports-cracks-down-on-information/))

- **Technology export ban remains in place** (from December 2023): China continues to prohibit the export of rare earth extraction, separation, and smelting technology — the core processing know-how that Western companies need to build their own separation facilities. ([AInvest](https://www.ainvest.com/news/china-address-rare-earth-concerns-changed-2605/))

- **Extraterritorial reach**: From December 1, 2026, foreign entities that manufacture products using Chinese rare earth technology, equipment, or materials will also require a Chinese export license — even if the transaction does not involve Chinese companies. ([TTWTO VCCI](https://wtocenter.vn/german-market/28826-china-expands-rare-earths-restrictions-targets-defense-and-chips-users))

### 2. The "May 2026" Connection — Suspension Window

The **November 2025 suspension** of certain rare earth export controls (the October 2025 expansion) runs **through November 2026**. During this window:

- China issued general licenses for U.S. end users
- The **April 2025 restrictions** on seven rare earth elements **remain in place**
- The **technology export ban** (December 2023) **remains in place**
- After **November 2026**, the second wave of controls can be reactivated without warning ([AInvest](https://www.ainvest.com/news/china-address-rare-earth-concerns-changed-2605/))

Analysts view this as a "tactical pause" rather than a substantive change.

### 3. Separation Technology — The Real Bottleneck

Multiple sources emphasize that **processing/separation — not mining — is the critical bottleneck**:

- China controls **~85–91%** of global rare earth separation capacity ([Mining SEE](https://www.miningsee.eu/rare-earth-supply-crunch-deepens-as-chinas-dominance-challenges-western-industrial-strategy/))

- Separation is the most **complex, capital-intensive** stage: requires hundreds of solvent extraction stages, hundreds of millions in upfront investment, and years to qualify products with magnet manufacturers ([Mining SEE](https://www.miningsee.eu/rare-earth-separation-outside-china-why-processing-not-mining-is-the-real-strategic-bottleneck-in-critical-minerals/))

- The Western technology gap is structural: **you cannot legally acquire the engineering to run separation facilities** from China due to the technology export ban ([AInvest](https://www.ainvest.com/news/china-address-rare-earth-concerns-changed-2605/))

### 4. Non-China Supply — Current Status

**Heavy rare earths** (dysprosium, terbium, yttrium) remain the most critical constraint:

- **McKinsey data**: By 2035, non-China supply of key heavy rare earths will still struggle to meet **20% of global demand** ([Chinatimes / Bloomberg](https://www.chinatimes.com/realtimenews/20260517000996-260409))

- **MP Materials** (U.S.): 40,000 tonnes total REO capacity (~11.5% global), but primarily **light** rare earths; its heavy separation facility targets only 3,000 tonnes/year input ([AInvest](https://www.ainvest.com/news/china-address-rare-earth-concerns-changed-2605/))

- **Lynas Rare Earths** (Australia/Malaysia): Achieved commercial production of separated heavy rare earths in May 2025, but measured in **hundreds of tonnes** vs. China's hundreds of thousands ([AInvest](https://www.ainvest.com/news/china-address-rare-earth-concerns-changed-2605/))

- **Japan's dependence** on China rebounded to **76%** as of January 2026, despite years of diversification efforts ([Chinatimes / Bloomberg](https://www.chinatimes.com/realtimenews/20260517000996-260409))

- **Europe** is wary of "market distortion" and higher costs from Western price floor mechanisms. European projects rely heavily on blended finance and state backing ([Mining SEE](https://www.miningsee.eu/rare-earth-supply-crunch-deepens-as-chinas-dominance-challenges-western-industrial-strategy/))

### 5. Emerging Technology: Modular Micro-Refineries

- **Silex World** (UK, spin-out from University of Leeds) has developed **modular micro-refineries** to recover rare earths from waste streams at source, using an alkali-based recovery process. This could reduce reliance on large centralized Chinese refineries. ([E&T Magazine](https://eandt.theiet.org/2026/05/22/modular-micro-refineries-extract-rare-earths-waste-streams-source))

**Key Takeaway**: As of **May 2026**, China retains near-total dominance over rare earth separation technology and capacity. The November 2025-March 2026 diplomatic talks produced only a **temporary suspension** of some controls (expiring November 2026), while the core technology export ban and structural processing advantages remain intact. Non-China alternatives (MP, Lynas) are scaling but remain marginal for heavy rare earths, and Japan's dependence has actually **rebounded** to 76%.

## Key Findings: Critical Minerals Policy Landscape (2026)

### 1. US Strategy: State-Led, Security-Focused

The Trump administration has significantly escalated the US approach to critical minerals, framing them as a **national security and industrial resilience priority**.

**Key legislative and executive actions:**
- **One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, July 2025):** Modified IRA tax credits (phasing out Section 45X starting 2031; ending 2034) but authorized major new funding:
  - $5 billion for an **Industrial Base Fund**
  - $2 billion for the **National Defense Stockpile Transaction Fund**
  - $500 million for **Defense Credit Programs** for critical minerals
- **Executive Orders:** EO 14154 ("Unleashing American Energy") and EO 14241 ("Immediate Measures to Increase American Mineral Production") streamlined permitting and used the **Defense Production Act (DPA)** to accelerate domestic projects.
- **"Project Vault":** A new strategic stockpile model making the US a structural buyer and holder of key materials.

**Defense Production Act (DPA) Usage (FY2025):** $550.4 million in aid for CRM projects (up from $209.2M in FY2024 and $313.6M in FY2023). At least 10 CRM companies supported since January 2025.

**DOE Loans & Major Deals:**
- **MP Materials (July 2025):** DoD invested $400M + $150M loan from Office of Strategic Capital for rare-earth separation at Mountain Pass. Included a 10-year NdPr price floor of $110/kg.
- **Lithium Americas:** $2.3 billion DOE loan restructuring with 5% equity stake.
- **Trilogy Metals:** 10% equity stake secured by US government.
- **Orion Resource Partners:** $5 billion critical minerals fund with US DFC.
- **Pinnacle/Atlantic Alumina:** $150M equity stake in gallium production facility.

**Mineral Diplomacy:** Signed **21 bilateral critical mineral frameworks or MOUs** with third countries since January 2025 (e.g., Ukraine, DRC, Australia, Japan, Kazakhstan).

### 2. EU Strategy: Market Mobilization & Integrated Industrial Policy

The EU is pursuing a **financially-driven and regulatory approach** under the **Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA)** and the **ReSourceEU Action Plan**.

**Key measures:**
- **47 Strategic Projects** within the EU (€22.5 billion total capital investment) covering lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese, graphite, rare earths, tungsten, magnesium.
- **13 Strategic Projects** in third countries (€5.5 billion needed).
- **EIB & EBRD Financing:** €2 billion for CRM investment in 2025; €100 million exploration facility under InvestEU; new CRM Task Force and one-stop shop.
- **ReSourceEU Action Plan (2026):** €3 billion investment drive focusing on de-risking and scaling extraction, processing, and recycling through a new **European Critical Raw Materials Centre**.
- **Offtake/Joint Purchasing:** EC Industry Commissioner Séjourné announced creation of a joint purchasing and strategic stockpiling centre "inspired by the Japanese model."

**International partnerships:**
- **South Africa:** Clean Trade and Investment Partnership with €750M commitment for infrastructure and mineral development emphasizing local processing.
- **Australia:** Ongoing negotiations for equity stakes and offtake agreements in lithium and rare earth projects backed by EIB.
- **Greenland Resources** (Malmbjerg molybdenum mine) expected to receive EIB financing.

### 3. US-EU Divergence & Coordination

**Key differences:**
| Dimension | US | EU |
|-----------|----|----|
| **Model** | Direct state ownership, equity stakes, price floors | Market mobilization, financial incentives, regulation |
| **Primary tools** | DPA, DoD/DoE grants, offtake agreements, CFIUS | CRMA, EIB/EBRD loans, Strategic Projects, FDI screening |
| **Focus** | National security, domestic production, allied sourcing | Domestic targets (2030 benchmarks), circular economy, ESG |
| **Capital deployed (2021-Feb 2026)** | ~€40 billion (~8x EU) | ~€5 billion |

**Coordination efforts (2026):**
- **US-EU Action Plan for Critical Minerals Supply Chain Resilience (April 24, 2026):** Framework for reference price tools, border adjusted price floors, standards-based markets, stockpiling cooperation, investment screening.
- **FORGE initiative** (February 2026): US-proposed allied framework.
- Ongoing discussions on **minimum price mechanisms** to counteract predatory pricing.

### 4. 2026 Developments & Outlook

- **US-EU Action Plan** signed April 2026 establishing transatlantic coordination on price tools, standards, and stockpiling.
- **Industrial Accelerator Act** (EU, March 4, 2026) opens door to "Buy European" or "trusted origin" requirements.
- **EU defense procurement rules revision** (planned later 2026) may introduce NDAA-style foreign entity-of-concern provisions.
- **Critical Mineral Dominance Act** (US, pending) would require identification of priority mining projects and expedited federal permitting.
- **EU FDI Regulation review** expected to introduce mandatory screening for critical raw materials.
- **Second call for Strategic Projects** under CRMA (deadline January 15, 2026) to expand the project pipeline.

### 5. Investment Implications

- **US projects:** Offer certainty through government backing but require alignment with federal priorities and CFIUS scrutiny for foreign investors.
- **EU projects:** Require compliance with ESG standards, cross-border coordination, and navigating fragmented permitting.
- **Blended finance** structures combining EU development banks with US-backed institutions are mobilizing €500M–€1B+ for strategically aligned projects.
- **Long-term offtake agreements** (based on the "Japanese model") are emerging as a key tool for both the US and EU to de-risk projects and secure supply.

### Bottom Line

The critical minerals landscape in 2026 is defined by **competing but parallel Western strategies**. The US is pursuing an aggressive, security-driven model with direct state intervention, equity stakes, and price floors via the DPA and DOE. The EU is building a regulatory and financial architecture (CRMA, ReSourceEU, EIB) emphasizing sustainability, circularity, and market mechanisms. Both are intensifying diplomatic outreach to resource-rich allies and tightening foreign investment screening. The **US-EU Action Plan** signals growing coordination, but fundamental differences in approach persist—creating both opportunities and compliance challenges for industry participants operating across both markets.
